client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. Some days it just hits me out of nowhere - I'll see something that reminds me of her and suddenly I can't stop crying. I know therapy is supposed to help, but I'm not sure talking about it will make the pain go away.
therapist: I hear how deeply this loss is affecting you—your voice sounds tender and rushed, like the grief is still very raw and close to the surface. It makes sense that reminders of your grandma bring such strong emotions, and it’s okay to feel unsure about whether talking will help—grief doesn’t follow a timeline, and healing often comes in waves. Would it help to explore what those painful moments are like for you, or how you might honor her memory in a way that feels meaningful?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if honoring her memory would help—sometimes I think it might just make me miss her more. When I see her favorite flowers or pass by her old house, the pain feels so sharp, like it just happened yesterday even though it's been months. Part of me wants to forget because remembering hurts so much, but then I feel guilty for even thinking that way.
therapist: Your voice sounds both shaky and urgent—like you're caught between wanting to hold onto her memory and fearing how much it hurts. That push-pull makes so much sense; grief isn’t just sadness, it’s love with nowhere to go right now. What if we gently explored how to carry both the pain *and* the warmth of her memory, rather than feeling like you have to choose one or the other?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I don't know if I can handle holding both at the same time. When I try to remember the good times, the pain of losing her just crashes over me like a wave. It feels easier to just shut down completely than to sit with that mix of love and hurt. 

I get what you're saying about not having to choose, but it's like my brain can't process both feelings together without short-circuiting. Maybe I'm just not strong enough for that approach.
therapist: Your voice sounds so strained and hurried—it’s clear this feels overwhelming and almost too much to hold. It’s not that you’re not strong enough; grief can feel like trying to hold onto two ends of a rope that’s pulling in opposite directions. Let’s slow this down and see if we can find small, manageable ways to approach these emotions, rather than feeling like you have to face them all at once. Would that feel safer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, slowing down sounds good in theory, but when I try, my brain just keeps racing. It's like there's a voice in my head saying "If you stop moving, everything will collapse." I know that's probably irrational, but it feels so real in the moment. Even sitting here now, part of me is screaming that we're wasting time by not rushing to "fix" everything immediately.
therapist: Your voice sounds both hurried and fragile—like you’re carrying this urgency and fear that things will fall apart if you don’t keep moving. That thought—“if I stop, everything collapses”—feels so real in the moment, doesn’t it? Let’s gently explore where that belief comes from and see if we can challenge it together, step by step, so it doesn’t feel so overwhelming.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, that does feel real. Like if I take even one day off from keeping everything together, my whole life will just... unravel. I don't know where it comes from exactly, but I remember my parents always being stretched so thin when I was growing up. Maybe that's part of it? But even knowing that doesn't make the feeling go away now. It's like my brain won't accept that things might actually be okay if I slow down.
therapist: Your voice sounds both hurried and tense—like this fear of unraveling is running in the background, even as you try to make sense of it. It’s understandable that growing up seeing your parents stretched thin might have shaped this belief that everything depends on you holding it all together. Let’s gently explore what might happen if you took small steps to slow down—not to fix everything at once, but to see if your brain might start to trust that slowing down doesn’t mean falling apart.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying about slowing down, but honestly the idea makes me really nervous. If I stop pushing myself so hard, doesn't that just mean things will pile up even more? 

I can already picture my to-do list growing out of control if I don't stay on top of everything. It feels like taking my foot off the gas pedal when I'm barely keeping the car on the road as it is.
therapist: Your voice sounds tight and rushed—like you're picturing everything spiraling if you ease up even a little. That image of barely keeping the car on the road shows how exhausting it feels to stay in this constant state of control. What if we tested that belief together—not by stopping all at once, but by seeing what happens when you loosen your grip just slightly on one small thing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, but the idea of loosening control even a little makes my chest feel tight. What if that one small thing I let go of turns out to be the thing that keeps everything from falling apart? I've had that happen before where I relaxed for just a moment and then everything got messy.
therapist: Your voice sounds higher and faster—I can hear how this thought instantly sets off that tight, anxious feeling. That fear of everything getting messy from just one small slip makes complete sense, especially when you’ve experienced it before. Let’s explore what “messy” actually looked like in those past moments—was it truly unmanageable, or might there have been ways to recover that your anxiety isn’t letting you see right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess the messy moments did feel unmanageable at the time, but looking back, I did get through them eventually. Still, it’s hard to remember that in the moment—it feels like everything will just spiral out of control. I don’t know if focusing on the past will help because every situation feels different now.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and higher-pitched—like even recalling past recoveries isn’t fully easing that fear of everything spiraling in new situations. That disconnect makes sense—when anxiety shouts, it’s hard to hear the quieter truth that you’ve gotten through tough moments before. What if we practice noticing small signs that *this* moment might be more manageable than your anxiety claims?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, I get what you're saying about looking for small signs, but when I'm in the middle of a panic, everything feels so overwhelming. It's like my brain just screams that this time is different, this time I won't be able to handle it. 

Even thinking about trying to notice small things makes me feel exhausted - like that's just one more thing to fail at when I'm already drowning.
therapist: Your voice sounds strained and hurried—I can hear how heavy this feels, like even the idea of trying something new adds to the weight instead of lifting it. That fear of failing when you’re already feeling overwhelmed makes complete sense, and it’s okay to feel exhausted by the thought of more effort. Let’s focus on what might feel doable, even if it’s just noticing one small thing without judgment—no pressure, no expectation, just curiosity.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It does feel heavy, like even small steps seem impossible right now. I want to try, but I keep thinking, “What if I fail again?” It’s hard to imagine curiosity helping when I’m stuck in this cycle of doubt and exhaustion. I guess I just don’t see how noticing one small thing could make a difference.
therapist: Your voice sounds both weary and higher-pitched—like the weight of past disappointments is making it hard to believe small steps could matter. That doubt makes so much sense when you’re stuck in this cycle, but what if we shifted the goal? Instead of aiming to "make a difference," could we simply notice one small thing—not to change anything, just to practice being present without judgment?
